about: The golden fixture volume set for the clean-room rewrite (issue #5, section 6.1). One volume per shape the format can take, so a baseline that passes across this set has been through every structural case the reader can meet. Each entry names the exact bundle file the registry serves for that slug -- the newest-wins fold picks it out of the many builds installed -- pinned by its manifest stamp and by the sha256 of the file itself. Classifications were verified by reading the manifests and world payloads out of the zips, not by reputation.
capturedFrom: ~/Library/Application Support/dev.felinestatemachine.atlas/bundles, except the city, which is built rather than installed and is read from its builtInto directory (ATLAS_GOLDEN_CITY_DIR overrides, as in golden/capture/capture.sh)
goldenTree: the current tree at branch m0/recapture

volumes.title: TUNIC
volumes.why: One world, one lens, one source. The baseline shape a MapGenie game arrives in: nothing merged, nothing split, nothing sharded, every collection a point collection drawn as pins.

volumes.title: Cyberpunk 2077
volumes.why: Two sources in one world. The merge ledger names Piggyback as the origin and IGN Wiki as a donor that matched 270 locations and added 37 of its own (alignment: 99 anchors, median 26.0px, p90 52.0px, worst 67.4px); the donor also arrives as a second lens over the same ground. Verified by reading worlds/night-city.json out of the zip -- the candidate was checked rather than assumed, and it does merge.

volumes.title: Fallout: New Vegas
volumes.why: Thirteen worlds, eight of them pieces cut from the Mojave sheet and carrying it as their parent. The split is the case where several places share one tile pyramid and the composer takes the sheet apart rather than showing it whole.

volumes.title: Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
volumes.why: The only installed volume whose lenses carry distinct shard ids -- Sky 1783, Surface 1784, Depths 1785 -- so a location belongs to one lens and switching lenses changes which features exist rather than only which raster is drawn. The suggested candidates (ghost-of-tsushima, sonic-frontiers, marathon) were inspected and all carry shard 0 on every lens; they are multi-world or multi-lens, not sharded.

volumes.title: Mars
volumes.why: The Trek planet: the only surface the viewer offers a globe for. It declares atlas.geometry.surface=sphere with an equirectangular mapping the viewer can invert, carries two lenses over the same ground, and declares a cell grid. Every globe-pane step in the tour is reachable only here.

volumes.title: Bend, Oregon
volumes.why: The only volume carrying all three geometries at once, and the only one with more than one shape-collection feature index: nine shape collections -- seven areas and two paths -- beside one point collection, 104 paths and 44 areas with their geometry inline. Three of the four national hydrography layers declare atlas.label.policy=quiet (Watersheds, Subwatersheds, Waterbodies; Streams declares none), which is the curation the label-policy ladder reads and the only real one in the set. Verified by reading atlas.json and worlds/2026-08-02.json out of the zip: one world, one lens, no shard, no split sheet -- the survey calls it plain, and what makes it the city fixture is its collections rather than its traits.
volumes.covers: the AND-highlight steps (and-highlighted, labels-held-highlighted, and-cleared), which need two feature indexes and had none in the public set, and the label ladder against declared policy rather than an empty ladder.
volumes.builtFor: the fixture set, not the library: the only city installed on this machine is a personal location whose name stays out of the repository, so this one was built from the public proof city by the reference tree's own pipeline (tools/crawl, tools/tiles, tools/generate -- golden/fixtures/README.md, 'The city fixture') into a directory outside the library, and is captured from there. The capture day is part of the identity: 2026-08-02 is the world's slug, the tile-set path and the bundle's version, so a re-crawl makes another world rather than this fixture.
volumes.gridNote: It declares a real-world window -- atlas.geometry.mercator.px and .deg -- but no atlas.geometry.projection, so the viewer reads no mapping over it and offers no cell grid: grid.enabled is false on every step, as on tunic. A rewrite that starts inferring the projection from the window would show up here as a changed field rather than as a changed step list.

privateVolumes.how: A volume that may not be named in the repository is described in the ignored FIXTURES.private.json and captured under --private, whose baselines go to the ignored golden/parity/private/.
privateVolumes.library: The private pass is additive: its volumes join the six public ones rather than standing in for the city, so it runs over a seven-volume library and its snapshots say so. A private baseline is a private record of the same tour, never diffed against a committed one, so it does not need the public library -- and a machine holding the private city really does have seven volumes on its select.
privateVolumes.wasTheCity: Before bend-or was built this file's city slot stood empty and the private city was the only volume filling that shape. The slot is now filled publicly; the private pass is extra coverage rather than a stand-in.

notChosen.finding: Two lenses, both shard 0, plus a MapGenie/IGN merge. A second merged volume, not a sharded one.
Four independent worlds, one lens each, all shard 0. Multi-world, not sharded and not split -- no world carries a parent.
Four independent worlds, one lens each, all shard 0.
Serves, but sorts first by title and so would silently become every unpinned tour's starting volume. The tour now pins its volume by slug, and tunic is the smaller plain case.
